When I moved from Boston to London to run a project for a bank, I thought the language would be the easy part. It was the hardest. In my first month, I sent a plan to a senior director, and he replied, 'Very interesting. I'd bear one or two things in mind.' I was delighted. I thought he loved it. Two weeks later, I found out that he had asked my boss to replace the whole plan. My British colleagues were not being dishonest. They were being tactful, and they expected me to understand. The opposite happened too. My emails were short and friendly by American standards, but people in the office found them curt. One colleague told me, very kindly, that I came across as angry. So I made two changes. I started every email with one sentence that had nothing to do with the task. And whenever a British colleague said that something was quite good, I asked a follow-up question. It saved me a lot of trouble.

I've been writing letters to the other side in disputes for almost thirty years, and the most useful thing I've learned is to take the person out of the problem. If I write, 'Your client failed to pay,' the other lawyer has to defend his client, and the next letter is angrier than mine. If I write, 'There has been a failure to pay the March invoice,' the facts are exactly the same, but there is nobody to defend. The noun does the work. The same is true of requests. 'Send me the documents now' starts a fight. 'We would be grateful for delivery of the documents by Friday' gets the documents. Young lawyers sometimes think this is weakness. It isn't. The firmness is in the deadline and in what happens after it, not in the adjectives. My letters are polite to the last line, and the last line is usually the date on which we will file the claim.
